content.text: A liveness probe answers "should this container be restarted?", and a readiness probe answers "should this Pod get traffic right now?". Point liveness at a check that includes your database, and a database outage makes every replica fail at once, so Kubernetes restarts the whole fleet. Keep liveness shallow, and put dependency checks in readiness, which takes a Pod out of rotation without killing it.

endpoint to its API that runs a quick query against the database, and wires it up as the liveness probe: if the API can't reach its data, it isn't healthy, so restart it. One evening the database fails over to a replica and is unreachable for a few minutes. Every API Pod fails the probe at the same moment, and every one is restarted, then restarted again. When the database is back, the API is still busy starting up. The incident review asks why Kubernetes made a short database blip so much worse.
The belief: an app has one health, so one
endpoint that checks everything it depends on is the best liveness probe. The deeper the check, the more problems it catches.

It's an understandable belief. "Health" sounds like a single yes-or-no answer, and many tutorials expose exactly one health endpoint. Deep checks really do catch more: an API that can't reach its database can't do its job. And restarting sometimes does help, for example when a process is stuck. So "unhealthy means restart" feels safe.
The half-truth: a deep check is a good signal. It's the wrong trigger for a restart, because restarting your process doesn't repair someone else's.
The kubelet runs each probe periodically on the container, and each one leads to a different action.
"determine when to restart a container", for example to catch "a deadlock, where an application is running, but unable to make progress." After
failures in a row, 3 by default, the container is restarted.
"determine when a container is ready to accept traffic." When one fails, the docs say the kubelet "continues running the container that failed checks" and sets the Pod's
condition to false. A startup probe holds back the other two until a slow app has finished starting.

Microsoft's Health Endpoint Monitoring pattern puts it in one line: "A responsive process isn't necessarily ready to serve requests, and restarting it doesn't repair a failed shared dependency." And a shared dependency fails for every replica at the same moment. The Kubernetes docs warn that liveness probes should "truly indicate unrecoverable application failure, for example a deadlock", and that "incorrect implementation of liveness probes can lead to cascading failures."
Readiness takes a Pod out of rotation
When readiness fails, the Pod stays listed in its Service's EndpointSlice with

. The EndpointSlice docs explain that the serving condition "maps to the Pod's Ready condition" and tells proxies whether the endpoint "should be used as a target for Service traffic." The container keeps its state, connections and warm caches, and gets traffic again as soon as the probe passes. The probe docs describe the pattern: "The liveness probe passes when the app itself is healthy, but the readiness probe additionally checks that each required back-end service is available."

content.text: In the first tab, both replicas restarted in lockstep, three times each in two and a half minutes. Their events read "Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503", then "Container api failed liveness probe, will be restarted". And because there was no readiness probe, both stayed
ready the whole time, so the Service kept sending them requests between restarts. In the second tab, both Pods went
with zero restarts. Note that the plain
table still lists both IPs; only the conditions show they're out of rotation. When the database returned, both were back in rotation seven seconds later, never having restarted.

blocks.title: You might not need liveness at all

content.text: The docs say that if your process "is able to crash on its own whenever it encounters an issue or becomes unhealthy, you do not necessarily need a liveness probe"; the kubelet restarts it according to the Pod's
. Add one when your app can hang without exiting, and make it check only that the process itself still responds.

blocks.title: Readiness on a shared dependency can still empty the Service

content.text: When every replica fails readiness at once, the Service has no ready endpoints. In our second tab, a client Pod calling the Service got

instead of a clear 503 from the API. Microsoft's pattern names the risk: a deep readiness probe against "an unreliable or slow dependency" can cause "a cascading failure where the monitoring mechanism reduces availability." Check only dependencies you truly can't work without, with short timeouts, and consider reporting degraded instead of not ready when you can still serve something useful.

items.title: Use a startup probe for slow starts

content.text: If startup is slow, don't stretch the liveness delay. Add a startup probe on the same cheap endpoint with a high
, so liveness only starts once the app is up.

items.title: Treat synchronized restarts as a probe bug

content.text: If every replica's RESTARTS count climbs together, check the events for "Liveness probe failed". The cause is almost always outside the Pods, and the probe is turning it into an outage.

items.text: Liveness decides restarts; readiness decides traffic. They answer different questions and need different checks.
A liveness probe that checks a shared dependency fails on every replica at once and restarts the whole fleet.
A failed readiness probe keeps the container running and marks its endpoint not ready until it passes again.
Keep liveness shallow, put required dependencies in readiness, and give every check a short timeout.
If all replicas fail readiness together, the Service has nothing to route to, so check only what you can't work without.
